posts.title: How to Record a Voiceover for a Video (Free, No App)
posts.metaTitle: How to Record a Voiceover for a Video (Free)
posts.description: Record a voiceover for a video on the timeline while it plays, make the voice clear, add music and captions — free in your browser, nothing uploaded.
posts.excerpt: Record a voiceover for a video right on the timeline while the pictures play, then clean it up, add music underneath and caption it — free in your browser.
posts.imageAlt: Record a voiceover: narration clip on audio track A2 with the Audio Track Mixer and mic buttons
posts.html:
A good narration turns a pile of clips into a story. This guide shows how to record a voiceover for a video right on the timeline — while the picture plays, so your words land on the right shots — and how to make it sound clean and clear afterwards. You only need a microphone (even the one in your headphones) and Reelsmith, a free editor that runs in your browser. The recording stays on your computer.

Before you record a voiceover

  • Write it down. Even a rough script stops the "um"s. Read it aloud once; spoken sentences should be short.
  • Pick a quiet, soft room. Curtains, a sofa or a wardrobe full of clothes absorb echo. Bare walls and tiles make it worse.
  • Get close to the microphone. About a hand's width away, a little to the side so your breath doesn't hit it.
  • Wear headphones. Then you hear yourself without the speakers leaking into the recording.

Step 1: Edit the pictures first

Open the editor, import your clips and put them in order on V1. It's much easier to talk over a finished cut than to cut pictures to fit a narration. Background music can wait until the end.

Step 2: Record the voiceover on the timeline

  1. Put the playhead where the narration should start.
  2. Click the mic button on an empty audio track's header (for example A2), or in the Audio Track Mixer.
  3. The first time, your browser asks for microphone access: click Allow.
  4. The program plays while you speak, so you can time your words to the pictures. The program's own sound is muted during recording to avoid echo.
  5. Press Space or click the mic again to stop.

The recording appears in the Project panel and on that track, starting at the playhead. See Recording a voice-over.

Tip: Record in short parts — one paragraph or one scene at a time. A mistake then costs ten seconds, not the whole take.

Step 3: Clean up the takes

  • Remove mistakes: press C for the razor, cut before and after the bad part, select it and press ⇧Delete to close the gap.
  • Fix the timing: drag a sentence left or right so it starts with the right shot.
  • Try again: record a new take on another audio track, then mute the track you don't want with M.

Step 4: Make the voice sound clear

  1. Even out the level: right-click the voice clip ▸ Normalize Loudness… and choose −14 LUFS, a common level for online video.
  2. Remove rumble: drag Effects ▸ Audio Effects ▸ High-Pass onto the clip. 80–100 Hz removes traffic, desk bumps and air-conditioning without thinning the voice.
  3. Smooth loud and quiet words: add the Compressor.
  4. Add clarity: in the Parametric EQ, raise High a little.

For background hiss and hum, see Audio effects: EQ, compressor, noise removal; for a quiet recording, how to make quiet audio louder.

Step 5: Add music under the voiceover

Put music on its own track, select it and apply Effects ▸ Smart Audio ▸ Auto Duck Music Under Voice. The music then dips automatically wherever you speak. The full method is in how to add music without drowning out your voice.

Step 6: Add captions from your voiceover

Many people watch without sound. Open the Captions tab and click Auto-generate: speech recognition runs on your own computer and turns your narration into captions you can edit (how auto captions work).

Voiceover tips that make a big difference

  • Smile while you talk. It sounds odd, but people can hear it (more about voice-over on Wikipedia).
  • Leave pauses. A beat of silence after an important line lets it sink in — and makes editing easier.
  • Drink water, not coffee or milk. They make the mouth sticky and noisy.
  • Keep the same distance from the microphone for the whole recording, so the sound doesn't change between takes.

Frequently asked questions

Why can't I hear the video while recording?

Reelsmith mutes the program sound during recording so it doesn't leak into your microphone. Use headphones if you want to hear it.

Which browser works best?

Chrome and Edge. Safari and Firefox work too; every browser asks for microphone permission once.

Can I import a voiceover I recorded on my phone?

Yes. Import the audio file (M4A, MP3 or WAV) and drag it onto an audio track.

Is my recording uploaded?

No. It is recorded and kept on your device.

Ready? Open the editor and record your first take.

posts.title: How to Make a Speed Ramp (Smooth Slow Motion, Free)
posts.metaTitle: How to Make a Speed Ramp (Free Slow Motion)
posts.description: Make a speed ramp step by step: Time Remap keyframes that slow the action down and speed it back up, plus slow and fast motion — free in your browser.
posts.excerpt: Make a speed ramp that slows down at the best moment and snaps back: Time Remap keyframes, plus simple slow and fast motion — free in your browser.
posts.imageAlt: Speed ramp with Time Remap Speed keyframes at 25% on a skateboarding clip in Effect Controls
posts.html:
A speed ramp is the move you see in every skate, sports and travel edit: the clip plays at normal speed, slows down right at the best moment, then snaps back. This guide shows how to make a speed ramp step by step with keyframes, and how to make simple slow motion and fast motion too. Everything works for free in Reelsmith, an editor that runs in your browser, with nothing uploaded.

Speed ramp, slow motion or fast motion?

  • Constant slow or fast motion changes the speed of a whole clip, for example 50% or 200%.
  • A speed ramp changes the speed gradually inside one clip, using keyframes. That's what makes it feel dynamic.

Both are in Effect Controls ▸ Time. Let's start with the simple one.

Constant slow motion or fast motion

  1. Open the editor, import your clip and drag it onto the timeline.
  2. Select the clip and open Effect Controls ▸ Time.
  3. Click a preset — 25%, 50%, 200% or 400% — or type any value into Speed.

Alternatively, press ⌘R (Ctrl+R on Windows) for Speed/Duration, where you can type a speed or a new length. Tick Ripple Edit, Shifting Trailing Clips there so later clips move along. Or use the Rate Stretch tool (R) and simply drag the clip's end: longer means slower. More in speed up a video.

How to make a speed ramp with keyframes

  1. Find the moment you want to slow down — the jump, the splash, the goal — and note where it starts and ends.
  2. Select the clip. In Effect Controls ▸ Time, move the playhead a little before the moment and click the stopwatch next to Time Remap Speed. This adds a keyframe at 100%.
  3. Move the playhead to where the action begins and set Time Remap Speed to 25–40%. A second keyframe appears.
  4. Move to where the action ends and add a keyframe with the same slow value, using the ◆ button.
  5. Move a little further and set the value back to 100% (or higher, for example 300%, for a fast exit).

The clip now shows TR on the timeline and the keyframes as small diamonds. Press Space to watch it. If the change feels abrupt, move the keyframes further apart; the ramp then takes longer. The details are in the time tools guide.

Tip: Put the slowest part exactly on the peak of the action — the top of the jump, the moment the ball leaves the foot. Ramp down just before it, not during it.

Tips for smooth slow motion

  • Film at a higher frame rate. Footage shot at 60 or 120 frames per second has more real frames to stretch, so slow motion stays fluid. Normal 30 fps footage at 25% shows each frame four times and can look choppy (why, on Wikipedia).
  • Keep the slow part short. One to three seconds of slow motion has the most impact.
  • Cut on the music. Put the ramp on a beat or a drop. The waveform on the audio track shows where the beats are.
  • Mute or replace the sound. Slowed sound rarely sounds good. Unlink with ⌘L and delete the clip's own audio, or let the music carry the moment.

Other time effects

  • Reverse: Effect Controls ▸ Time ▸ Reverse plays the clip backwards — fun for a rewind moment. See reverse a video.
  • Freeze frame: Frame Hold stops the picture on one frame, for example to introduce a person.

Frequently asked questions

Why doesn't my speed ramp show up?

Time Remap needs at least two keyframes with different values. Check that the stopwatch is on (orange) and that the diamonds sit inside the clip.

How do I remove a speed ramp?

Click the stopwatch next to Time Remap Speed again. The keyframes are removed and the clip keeps a single speed.

Can I ramp the audio too?

Speed changes apply to the clip's linked sound as well. For most edits, though, music on its own track sounds better.

Is my video uploaded?

No. Editing and exporting happen in your browser, on your own device.

Ready? Open the editor and try a ramp on your best clip.

posts.title: How to Blur a Face in a Video (and Make It Follow the Person)
posts.metaTitle: How to Blur a Face in a Video (Free)
posts.description: Blur a face in a video for free: a pixelated copy, an ellipse mask and tracking that follows the person — in your browser, with your footage never uploaded.
posts.excerpt: Blur a face in a video so it stays hidden while the person moves: a blurred copy, an ellipse mask and tracking — free in your browser, with nothing uploaded.
posts.imageAlt: Blur a face in a video: pixelated face inside an ellipse mask with the mask settings in Effect Controls
posts.html:
Filmed someone who didn't agree to be in your video? Or a licence plate, a house number or a screen with private details? This guide shows how to blur a face in a video so it stays hidden even while the person moves: a blurred copy of the clip, a mask around the face, and tracking that makes the mask follow. It all works for free in Reelsmith, an editor that runs in your browser — handy for exactly this job, because the footage never leaves your computer.

How blurring a face works

You stack two copies of the same clip. The bottom copy (V1) stays sharp. The top copy (V2) gets a blur or pixelation effect, and a mask cuts it down to an oval around the face. As a result, you see the sharp video everywhere except inside the mask. Then tracking moves the mask with the face.

Step 1: Duplicate the clip onto V2

  1. Open the editor, import your video and drag it onto V1.
  2. Hold Alt (Option on a Mac) and drag the clip straight up onto V2. That makes an exact copy, lined up in time.
  3. Optionally, delete the copy's audio clip so the sound isn't doubled: Alt-click it and press Delete.

Step 2: Blur the copy

Open Effects ▸ Video Effects and drag Mosaic onto the V2 clip for the classic pixelated look. Alternatively, use Effects ▸ Blur & Motion ▸ Gaussian Blur for a soft blur. For now the whole picture is blurred — the mask fixes that next.

Tip: Pixelation hides a face more reliably than a light blur. If you use Gaussian Blur, raise the amount until the face is truly unrecognisable.

Step 3: Draw a mask around the face

  1. Select the V2 clip and open Effect Controls ▸ Opacity ▸ Masks.
  2. Click Ellipse. An oval appears in the Program monitor.
  3. Click Edit on the mask, then drag inside it to move it over the face and drag the corner handles to fit. Keep it a little larger than the face.
  4. Raise Feather to soften the edge, so the blur doesn't end in a hard line.

Now only the face is blurred. For odd shapes, use the Pen tool (P) and click points around the area instead. See Masks.

Step 4: Make the blur follow the face

  1. Move the playhead to the first frame where the face is visible.
  2. On the mask in Effect Controls, click Track ▶.
  3. A progress window shows the frames being analysed. When it finishes, the mask moves with the face to the end of the clip.

Play it back and check every second. Tracking works best on faces with clear detail and steady light; it follows position, not size, so if the person walks toward the camera, keep the mask generous. If the tracking slips, click Clear track, move the playhead to where it went wrong, and track again from there. More in Tracking a mask.

Blur several faces or objects

  • Two faces at once: add a second mask to the same V2 clip. Masks on one clip combine.
  • A face that appears only briefly: cut the V2 copy with the razor (C) so it only covers those seconds.
  • Everything except one person: tick Inverted on the mask to blur the background instead.

Is blurring enough to protect someone?

Usually, but not always. A light blur can sometimes be partly reversed, and people can still be recognised by their voice, clothes or surroundings (more about pixelization on Wikipedia). Therefore use strong Mosaic, cover the whole head, and consider cutting the scene if the person remains easy to identify. When in doubt, ask for permission.

Frequently asked questions

Can I blur a licence plate or a screen the same way?

Yes. Use a Rectangle mask instead of an ellipse and track it like a face.

Why is the whole video blurred?

The blur effect is on the V2 copy, but the mask is missing or on the wrong clip. Select the V2 clip and add the mask there.

Can I blur the background instead of a face?

Yes — tick Inverted on the mask. For a vertical video with blurred bars at the sides, see blur a video background.

Is my video uploaded to blur it?

No. Masking, tracking and exporting all happen on your device, which matters when the footage is private.

Ready? Open the editor and blur your first face in a couple of minutes.

posts.title: How to Color Correct a Video (Free, in Your Browser)
posts.metaTitle: How to Color Correct a Video (Free)
posts.description: Color correct a video for free: fix white balance, exposure and contrast, add colour and match every clip with Lumetri Color in your browser — no upload.
posts.excerpt: Color correct a video step by step: fix the white balance, set exposure and contrast, bring back colour and make every clip match — with Lumetri Color, free in your browser.
posts.imageAlt: Color correct a video with Lumetri Color: temperature, contrast, highlights and saturation in Effect Controls
posts.html:
Phone and camera footage often comes out a little flat, too blue or too dark. This guide shows how to color correct a video in a few minutes: fix the white balance, set the exposure and contrast, bring back colour, and keep every clip in a scene looking the same. You'll use Lumetri Color in Reelsmith, a free editor that runs in your browser, so your footage is never uploaded.

Color correction is not the same as a "look". First you make the picture natural and consistent; only then, if you like, you add a style on top.

Before you color correct a video

  • Correct one clip at a time. Each shot was lit differently, so each needs its own settings.
  • Watch the scopes, not just the picture. Screens differ in brightness; the Lumetri Scopes tab measures the image instead.
  • Work in order: white balance, then exposure and contrast, then saturation. Each step changes how the next one looks.

Step 1: Open Lumetri Color

  1. Open the editor, click Import and drag your clips onto the timeline.
  2. Click the first clip to select it.
  3. In Effect Controls, open the Lumetri Color section. Its first part, Basic Correction, has everything this guide needs.

Step 2: Fix the white balance

White balance decides whether white looks white. Footage shot indoors often looks orange, and shade or cloudy days look blue.

  • Temperature moves the picture from cooler (blue) to warmer (orange). If the clip looks cold, move it right; if it looks yellow, move it left.
  • Tint fixes a green or magenta cast, which fluorescent lights often cause.

Look at something that should be neutral, such as a white wall, a grey road or a cloud. When it stops looking tinted, the white balance is right.

Step 3: Set exposure and contrast

  1. Exposure brightens or darkens the whole picture, in stops. Small steps go a long way, so try 0.2 or 0.3 first.
  2. Contrast makes darks darker and brights brighter. Flat footage usually needs a little more.
  3. Highlights brings back detail in bright areas, such as a sky; pull it down if the clouds look like white paper.
  4. Shadows opens up dark areas without making the whole image grey.
  5. Whites and Blacks set the brightest and darkest points. A slightly lower Blacks value adds depth.

Tip: Open the Lumetri Scopes tab while you adjust. The waveform should spread from near the bottom to near the top without being cut off at either end.

Step 4: Bring back the colour

Next, raise Saturation a little, to about 105–120%, if the clip still looks dull. Watch skin tones: when faces turn orange, you've gone too far. In contrast, lowering saturation calms down a busy, colourful scene; 0% makes it black and white.

Step 5: Fine-tune with curves and color wheels

  • Curves: click the master curve to add a point and drag it. A gentle S-shape adds contrast; raising the middle brightens mid-tones only. The Red, Green and Blue curves fix a colour cast in one range.
  • Color Wheels: drag the centre dot of Shadows, Midtones or Highlights toward a colour to tint just that range — for example, slightly blue shadows and warm highlights.
  • Vignette darkens the edges to draw the eye to the centre. Use it lightly.

Every control is explained in Lumetri Color, and the scopes in Lumetri Scopes.

Step 6: Make every clip match

A scene looks wrong when one shot is warmer than the next. Therefore, compare clips side by side: put the playhead on a corrected clip, look at its scopes, then move to the next clip and adjust it until the waveform and colours sit in the same place.

For a whole section, use an adjustment layer instead: Sequence ▸ Add Adjustment Layer, stretch it over the clips and apply Lumetri Color to it once. Everything below it changes together. See Adjustment layers.

Color correction vs color grading

Color correction makes footage look natural and consistent. Color grading then gives it a mood, such as warm and nostalgic or cold and tense (background on Wikipedia). In Reelsmith, Effects ▸ Filters has one-click looks like Cinematic, Teal & Orange and Golden Hour. Apply one after you correct, then fine-tune it in Lumetri Color.

Common mistakes

  • Too much saturation. It looks great for a second, then cheap. Skin tones are the first warning.
  • Crushed blacks. If shadows turn into one black blob, raise Blacks or Shadows.
  • Correcting on a very bright or very dark screen. Check the scopes and, if you can, look at the export on a phone too.

Frequently asked questions

Can I use one color correction for several clips?

Yes. Put an adjustment layer over the clips and apply Lumetri Color to it once (step 6). Clips that need extra work can still get their own correction underneath.

How do I reset a clip's colour?

Click Reset Lumetri at the bottom of the Lumetri Color section.

Does color correction slow down the export?

Hardly. The colour work runs on your graphics chip, both in the preview and in the export.

Is my video uploaded when I color correct it?

No. Everything, including the export, happens on your own device.

Ready? Open the editor, or read how to export a smaller file without losing quality once your colours are right.

posts.title: How to Add Music to a Video Without Drowning Out Your Voice
posts.metaTitle: Add Music to a Video Without Drowning Your Voice
posts.description: Add music to a video so your voice stays clear: a separate track, fades, automatic ducking under speech and an even mix — free, in your browser, no upload.
posts.excerpt: Add background music that sits under your voice: put it on its own track, fade it, let Auto Duck lower it while you speak and balance the mix — free, in your browser.
posts.imageAlt: Add music to a video: voice and background music on separate tracks with Auto Duck keyframes
posts.html:
Music makes a video feel finished — but only if people can still hear what you say. This guide shows how to add music to a video so it sits under your voice instead of fighting it: put it on its own track, fade it in and out, let the editor lower it automatically while you speak, and balance the final mix. Everything happens for free in Reelsmith, an editor that runs in your browser, so your files are never uploaded.

Also, the same steps work for a vlog, a tutorial, a product video or a podcast clip.

Before you add music to a video: get the rights

Only use music you are allowed to use. Popular songs can get your video muted, blocked or monetised by someone else. For example, YouTube's Audio Library offers royalty-free music and sound effects for creators; some tracks require a credit in your video's description, so check each one (YouTube Help: Audio Library). Other good sources are music you made yourself or tracks you licensed.

Step 1: Import the video and the music

  1. Open the editor and click Import. Select your video and the music file — MP3, WAV and M4A all work.
  2. Drag the video onto V1. Its own sound (your voice) lands on A1.
  3. Drag the music onto the empty track below, A2.

Tip: Keep voice and music on separate audio tracks. That way you can mute, solo or adjust each one on its own, and Auto Duck can tell them apart.

Step 2: Make the music fit the video

  • Too long? Drag the end of the music clip to where the video ends, or press C for the razor tool, cut, and delete the rest.
  • Too short? In that case, drag the song onto the timeline a second time, right after the first, and blend the joint with a crossfade (step 3).
  • Starts in the wrong place? Slide the clip left so the music starts at a strong moment, then trim the beginning.

Step 3: Fade the music in and out

An abrupt start or stop sounds like a mistake. Select the music clip and set Fade In and Fade Out in Effect Controls ▸ Audio — one to three seconds usually feels natural. Alternatively, drag Constant Power from the audio transitions onto the clip's edge; between two music clips, it makes a smooth crossfade.

Step 4: Lower the music automatically while you speak

This is the step that keeps your voice clear. Select the music clip and apply Effects ▸ Smart Audio ▸ Auto Duck Music Under Voice. Reelsmith finds where someone speaks on the other audio tracks and lowers the music there by 14 dB, with smooth ramps in and out. As a result, the music fills the pauses and steps back during speech — just like on TV.

The dips are ordinary volume keyframes, so you can still change them: select the music, open Effect Controls ▸ Audio ▸ Volume and move or delete keyframes. More in Voice effects, sound effects and auto ducking.

Step 5: Balance the voice and the music

  1. Even out the voice: right-click your voice clip ▸ Normalize Loudness… and choose −14 LUFS, the usual level for YouTube and most online video.
  2. Set the music level: lower the music clip's Volume in Effect Controls, or pull down the A2 fader in the Audio Track Mixer, until the music supports the voice without competing.
  3. Check the meters on the right of the timeline while you play: keep the peaks below 0, because the top turns red near clipping.

Then listen once on headphones and once on a phone speaker. If you can understand every word on the phone, the mix is right. For quiet recordings, see how to make quiet audio louder, and for all mixing tools Audio mixing.

Step 6: Export the video with music

Click Export, choose a preset — for example YouTube 1080p Full HD — and click Export. Every unmuted audio track is mixed into the file with its volume, fades and ducking. In addition, File ▸ Export Audio… saves just the soundtrack as M4A or WAV if you need it separately.

Tips for choosing background music

  • Match the mood and the pace. Calm music for tutorials, upbeat music for vlogs and montages.
  • Prefer instrumentals under speech. After all, lyrics compete with your words, so save vocal tracks for parts without talking.
  • Cut on the beat. The waveform shows the beats; cutting your video there makes the edit feel deliberate.
  • Use sound effects sparingly. For instance, Effects ▸ Sound Effects has original whooshes, pops and dings that are free to use in your videos.

Frequently asked questions

Can I add music to a video and remove the original sound?

Yes. Select the clip, unlink video and audio with ⌘L (Ctrl+L on Windows), select the original audio and press Delete. See remove audio from a video.

Can I use more than one song?

Yes. Place songs one after another on the music track and crossfade them with Constant Power, or put a second song on another audio track.

Why is my music still too loud?

Auto Duck lowers the music only while someone speaks. Therefore, if it is too loud between sentences, lower the music clip's overall volume as well.

Is my video uploaded when I add music?

No. Importing, mixing and exporting all happen on your device.

Ready? Try the free background music tool, or open the editor.

posts.title: How to Turn a Video into a GIF (Free, Small and Sharp)
posts.metaTitle: How to Turn a Video into a GIF (Free)
posts.description: Turn a video into a GIF for free: mark the moment, choose size and frame rate, add text and export a small, sharp loop in your browser — nothing uploaded.
posts.excerpt: Turn a video into a GIF in a few clicks: mark the moment, pick the size and frame rate, add a caption and export a small, sharp looping GIF — free, in your browser.
posts.imageAlt: Turn a video into a GIF: Export as GIF settings with an In/Out range, 480 px wide and 15 fps
keywords: make a gif from a video
posts.html:
A GIF is the easiest way to share a reaction, a quick how-to or a product demo: it plays on its own, loops forever and works almost everywhere. This guide shows how to turn a video into a GIF in a few clicks — pick the moment, choose the size and frame rate, and export. You can do it for free in Reelsmith, an editor that runs in your browser, so your video is never uploaded.

In addition, you'll learn how to keep the file small and sharp, because GIFs grow large quickly if you aren't careful.

When a GIF is better than a video

  • Short loops: reactions, a funny moment, a logo animation.
  • Quick demos: a click in an app, a before-and-after, a cooking step.
  • Places without video: some documentation tools, forums and email newsletters show GIFs but not video players.

However, for anything longer than about 20 seconds, or anything that needs sound, an MP4 is the better choice — it is much smaller and keeps the audio.

Step 1: Import the video

  1. Open the editor and click Import, or drag the file onto the window.
  2. Drag the clip onto the timeline. Any format your browser can play works, including MP4, MOV and WebM.

Step 2: Mark the part you want to turn into a GIF

  1. Play the video and stop just before the moment starts.
  2. Press I to set the In point, play to the end of the moment, then press O to set the Out point.
  3. Then keep it short: two to six seconds is ideal for a loop.

More about In and Out points: Markers and In/Out. Alternatively, cut the clip itself — see trim a video.

Tip: A loop feels smoother when the last frame looks like the first. Move the Out point a frame or two until the jump disappears.

Step 3: Add text (optional)

Reaction GIFs often have a caption. Press T, click in the Program monitor and type, then style it in Effects ▸ Text Styles. Titles and captions that are visible in the Program monitor are included in the GIF. See how to make animated text for more.

Step 4: Export the video as a GIF

  1. Choose File ▸ Export as GIF….
  2. Set Range to Sequence In/Out to use the part you marked (or keep the whole sequence).
  3. Choose the Size: 320, 480, 640 or 800 px wide. The height follows your video's shape.
  4. Choose the Frame rate: 10, 15, 20 or 25 fps.
  5. Keep Loop forever ticked, name the file and click Export GIF.

The line under the settings shows the final size, length and number of frames before you export. All of it runs on your own device. See Export as GIF and audio for the details.

How to keep a GIF small and sharp

The GIF format is old and simple: it stores every frame as an image with at most 256 colours (background on Wikipedia). Therefore size grows fast with length, size and frame rate. A few rules help:

  • Shorter is better. After all, every second adds 10–25 more images.
  • 480 px wide is usually plenty for chats and most web pages; use 640 or 800 only where it is shown large.
  • 15 fps looks smooth for most motion. For example, a screen recording is often fine at 10 fps.
  • Still backgrounds are cheap. Reelsmith merges frames that don't change, so a tripod shot or a screen demo stays small.
  • Avoid big gradients. Skies and soft lighting show banding with only 256 colours; strong, flat colours look best.

Turn a video into a GIF for different places

  • Chat and social replies: 480 px, 15 fps, 2–4 seconds.
  • Documentation and help pages: 640 or 800 px, 10 fps, so text in the screen recording stays readable.
  • Email newsletters: 480 px and as short as possible, because many email apps load images slowly.

Fixing common GIF problems

  • The file is too big. First shorten the range, then choose a smaller width; after that, lower the frame rate. As a result, a 10 MB GIF often drops below 3 MB without looking worse.
  • Colours look blotchy. This happens in gradients such as skies. Instead, pick a moment with flatter colours, or brighten the clip a little in Lumetri Color before exporting.
  • The motion looks choppy. Raise the frame rate to 20 or 25 fps for fast movement. On the other hand, keep the GIF short so the extra frames don't make it huge.
  • The loop jumps. Move the In or Out point by a frame or two, or end on a frame that matches the start.

Frequently asked questions

Does a GIF have sound?

No. The GIF format has no audio. If you need sound, export an MP4 instead — it is also smaller.

How long can a GIF be?

There is no fixed limit, but files grow quickly. Above about 20 seconds, Reelsmith suggests an MP4, which is usually much smaller.

Can I turn a video into a GIF on my phone?

Yes. Reelsmith works in mobile browsers: import the clip, set In and Out, and choose Export as GIF from the File menu.

Is my video uploaded when I turn a video into a GIF?

No. The GIF is made in your browser, and the file is saved straight to your device.

Try it now with the free video to GIF converter, or open the editor.

posts.html:
Need a smaller file for email, a chat app or a slow upload? This guide shows how to compress a video without losing quality you can actually see — by choosing the right frame size and quality, and checking the file size before you export. It all happens in Reelsmith, a free editor that runs in your browser, so your video is never uploaded anywhere.

No compression is truly lossless. However, a phone or laptop screen can't show most of the detail a camera records, so a well-chosen smaller file looks the same to viewers at a fraction of the size.

What decides the size of a video file

Three things decide how big an exported video is:

  • Length. For example, twice as long means twice as big. Cutting what nobody needs is the only compression that loses nothing at all.
  • Bitrate (Quality). How much data each second gets. In other words, this is the biggest lever.
  • Frame size (resolution). 1280×720 has less than half the pixels of 1920×1080; therefore it needs much less data for the same sharpness.

As a result, the best way to compress a video without losing quality is to trim first, then lower the resolution a step, and only then lower the quality.

Step 1: Trim before you compress a video

  1. Open the editor, click Import and drag your video onto the timeline.
  2. Cut the slow start and the end: press C for the razor tool, click where the good part begins, then select the piece before it and press ⇧Delete (Ripple Delete).
  3. Also, want to keep the timeline but export only one part? Set In and Out points with I and O and choose Range ▸ Sequence In/Out when you export.

More ways to shorten a clip: trim a video online.

Step 2: Open Export and choose Custom

Click Export in the top right (or press ⌘M). For a quick small file, the Review copy (small file) preset is enough. However, for more control, set Preset to Custom and follow the next two steps.

Step 3: Choose a smaller frame size

Open Frame size and pick 1280×720 — HD. For most videos watched on phones, laptops or in chats, 720p still looks sharp. On the other hand, keep 1920×1080 — Full HD for YouTube uploads and big screens.

Tip: Never pick a frame size larger than your original. Scaling up makes the file bigger without adding any detail.

Step 4: Choose the quality and compress the video

Quality has three levels: High, Medium and Low (small file). Medium is the sweet spot for most videos; in contrast, Low is fine for talking heads, slides and screen recordings, where little moves.

Approximate size per minute at 30 frames per second, as the Export dialog estimates it:

Frame sizeHighMediumLow
1920×108064 MB37 MB21 MB
1280×72029 MB17 MB12 MB

Real files can come out a little different, because the encoder spends fewer bits on simple scenes.

Step 5: Check the estimate and compress the video

  1. Look at the summary at the bottom of the dialog: it shows the frame size, the range and the Estimated file size, updated as you change settings.
  2. Too big? Then lower the quality one step or shorten the range, and watch the estimate drop.
  3. Finally, click Export. Compression runs on your own computer, usually much faster than real time.

Every setting is explained in Exporting a video.

MP4 or WebM: which format is smaller?

H.264 (.mp4) plays everywhere — phones, TVs, email previews and every social app — so it is the safe choice. VP9 (.webm), by comparison, is often a little smaller at the same quality, and it is fine for websites and Chrome-based apps. Which formats appear depends on what your browser can encode.

How small does it need to be?

  • Email: personal Gmail accounts can attach up to 25 MB, and bigger files are sent as a Google Drive link instead (Gmail Help). A two-minute clip at 1280×720 and Low quality fits.
  • Chat apps: 720p at Medium usually looks clean on a phone. Most apps also compress again when you send, so starting from a clean 720p file avoids a second, blurrier round.
  • YouTube and Vimeo: don't compress much at all — the platform compresses again, so upload a high-quality file.

Mistakes that cost quality

  • Compressing twice. Each round throws away more detail. Always export from the original file.
  • Shrinking the frame too far. Below 720p, text and faces start to look soft.
  • Starving fast motion. Sports and gaming need more data, so use Medium or High for them.
  • Forgetting the sound. Audio is a small part of the file, so there is no need to remove it to save space. Instead, cut silent parts of the video itself.

Frequently asked questions

Can I compress a video without losing quality at all?

Only by cutting it shorter. Any lower bitrate or resolution removes some data, but at sensible settings the difference is invisible on a normal screen.

Is my video uploaded when I compress it?

No. Reelsmith reads the file from your computer and encodes it there. Read why your videos never leave your computer.

How long does it take to compress a video?

Usually less than the length of the video. Because Reelsmith encodes on your own graphics hardware, a two-minute clip at 720p often takes well under a minute on a recent laptop. Older computers and phones are slower, and the progress window shows the speed while it works.

Can I compress several videos at once?

Export them one after another: import each video, put it on the timeline and export. It usually takes seconds.

Does it work on a phone?

Yes. The editor works in mobile browsers; big 4K files are smoother on a computer.

Ready? Use the free video compressor, or resize the video for a specific platform first.

posts.title: How to Turn a Long Video into Shorts (Free, in Your Browser)
posts.metaTitle: Turn a Long Video into Shorts (Free Guide)
posts.description: Turn a long video into Shorts: mark the best moments, cut each into its own 9:16 sequence, fill the frame, add captions and export — free, in your browser.
posts.excerpt: Turn one long video into several Shorts: mark the best moments, give each its own vertical sequence, fill the frame, add captions and export them all — free, with nothing uploaded.
posts.imageAlt: Turn a long video into Shorts: markers on the best moments, a vertical Short sequence tab and an In/Out range in the Source monitor
posts.html:
One good long video can become five or ten Shorts. This guide shows how to turn a long video into Shorts — a podcast, a tutorial, a stream or a vlog — by marking the best moments, cutting each one into its own vertical sequence and exporting them in one sitting. It all happens in Reelsmith, a free editor in your browser, so even a two-hour recording is never uploaded anywhere.

Repurposing works because the hard part, recording something worth watching, is already done. In addition, Shorts bring new viewers to your long videos, so each clip should make people curious about the full episode.

What makes a good moment when you repurpose long videos

Look for parts that make sense on their own, without the rest of the video:

  • One clear tip or answer — "the one setting that fixed my audio".
  • A strong reaction — surprise, a laugh, a disagreement.
  • A before-and-after or a result you can show in the first second.
  • A bold statement that people want to comment on.

Aim for 15–45 seconds each. If a moment needs a long introduction, it is probably not a Short — and that is fine, because the goal when you turn a long video into Shorts is quality, not quantity.

Step 1: Import the long video and mark the best moments

  1. Open the editor, import your recording and drag it onto the timeline.
  2. Play through it. Whenever something good happens, press M to add a marker at the playhead.
  3. Double-click a marker in the ruler to name it — for example Best tip or Funny moment — and give it a colour.
  4. Press ⇧M to jump from one marker to the next when you come back to them.

Tip: Press L twice to play at double speed while you look for moments; K stops. Long recordings go much faster this way.

Step 2: Make a vertical sequence for each Short

  1. Choose Sequence ▸ New Sequence… and name it after the moment, for example Short 1 — Best tip.
  2. Open Sequence ▸ Sequence Settings…, pick Vertical 9:16 (1080×1920) and untick Match frame size to the first video clip. Otherwise the landscape footage would switch the sequence back to 16:9.
  3. Click Apply. The new sequence opens as a tab above the timeline, next to your full video.

Step 3: Bring the moment into the Short

  1. Double-click the long video in the Project panel to open it in the Source monitor.
  2. Find the moment, click inside the Source monitor and press I at the start and O at the end.
  3. Click the timeline of your Short sequence and press , (Insert). Only the marked part is added.

Each Short has its own tab, so you can switch between them while you work. More detail: the Source monitor and multiple sequences.

Step 4: Fill the vertical frame

A landscape clip sits in the middle of a 9:16 frame with empty space above and below. You have two good options:

  • Crop in: select the clip and tick Scale to fill frame in Effect Controls ▸ Motion, then drag the picture so the speaker's face is centred.
  • Keep everything: drag Background Blur Fill from Effects ▸ Creative Effects onto the clip. The whole picture stays visible over a blurred copy — ideal for screen recordings and wide shots with two people.

The blurred background tool and the vertical video guide show both in more detail.

Step 5: Tighten it and add a hook

  • Cut the warm-up. Start on the most interesting sentence, even if it is mid-thought.
  • Remove pauses with the razor tool (C) and Ripple Delete (⇧Delete).
  • Press T and type a short hook at the top, such as "Nobody tells you this". Click Safe under the monitor to keep it clear of YouTube's buttons.

Step 6: Add captions to every Short

Open the Captions tab and click Auto-generate with Entire sequence selected. Each Short gets its own captions, made on your device. Then click Style… for larger text with a box, and move them up with the margin so they sit above the app's controls. See how to add subtitles automatically.

Step 7: Export all your Shorts

  1. Click a Short's tab, then Export, and choose YouTube Shorts / Reels / TikTok (9:16).
  2. Name the file after the moment and click Export.
  3. Repeat for each tab. Exports run on your own computer, so each one usually takes seconds.
  4. Upload them from the YouTube app or YouTube Studio — YouTube lists its current rules in Upload YouTube Shorts.

Tip: Upload the Shorts over several days rather than all at once, and mention the full video in each one — for example "full episode on my channel".

A quicker way to turn a long video into Shorts (one clip)

Need just one Short? Skip the extra sequences: set In and Out points on the long video's timeline with I and O, and choose Range ▸ Sequence In/Out in the export settings. Pair it with the YouTube Shorts / Reels / TikTok (9:16) preset and Background Blur Fill for a fast result.

Frequently asked questions

How many Shorts can I make from one long video?

As many as it has self-contained moments. A one-hour podcast often gives five to ten good clips; a ten-minute tutorial perhaps two or three.

Can I turn a long video into Shorts without cropping out people?

Yes. Use Background Blur Fill, which keeps the whole frame visible, or place two clips above each other for a split screen.

Is there a length limit when I repurpose long videos?

No server limit, because the file opens from your own computer. Very long 4K recordings are smoother on a computer with plenty of memory; proxies help on slower machines.

Do the Shorts need their own captions?

Yes — generate them per Short. It is quick, and each clip then works with the sound off.

Next, polish each clip with how to edit YouTube Shorts, or open the editor and start with your latest video.

posts.title: How to Edit YouTube Shorts: A Free Step-by-Step Workflow
posts.metaTitle: How to Edit YouTube Shorts (Free, Step by Step)
posts.description: How to edit YouTube Shorts for free: a 9:16 template, tight cuts, a hook title, auto captions, effects, even sound and the right export — in your browser.
posts.excerpt: Edit a YouTube Short from raw clips to upload in about fifteen minutes: template, tight cuts, hook title, captions, effects, clean sound and a 9:16 export — free, in your browser.
posts.imageAlt: Edit YouTube Shorts with a 9:16 template: hook title, progress bar and follow button
keywords: how to make a youtube short
posts.html:
Want to edit YouTube Shorts that people actually watch to the end? This guide takes one Short from raw phone clips to a finished upload in about fifteen minutes, using Reelsmith — a free editor that runs in your browser, with no upload and no watermark. Every step uses a real button in the editor, so you can follow along.

The workflow works the same for Instagram Reels and TikTok, because all three use the same vertical 9:16 format.

Before you edit YouTube Shorts: plan in one sentence

Good Shorts are about one thing. Before you open the editor, finish this sentence: "By the end, the viewer will…" — know a trick, see a result, laugh at a reaction. Everything that doesn't serve that sentence gets cut. As a result, the edit becomes much faster, because you already know what to keep.

Step 1: Start from the Shorts template

  1. Open the editor. On the start screen, under Start from a template, click Shorts / Reels / TikTok.
  2. You get a 1080×1920 sequence with a hook title, a Progress Bar and a Follow Button already placed. V1 is left empty for your video.
  3. Click Import video in the guide (or drag files onto the window) and drag your clips onto V1.

The template keeps the vertical frame even if you drop in landscape footage. Prefer to start from scratch? How to make vertical videos explains the frame settings.

Step 2: Cut it tight

Shorts are judged in the first seconds, so the edit should never pause.

  • Press C for the razor tool and click at the start and end of every pause or stumble.
  • Press V, select the piece you don't want and press ⇧Delete (Ripple Delete) — the gap closes on its own.
  • Move your best moment to the very start. For example, show the finished result first and explain how afterwards.

Tip: Zoom the timeline with = and − to cut word by word. The audio waveform shows exactly where each pause is.

Step 3: Write the hook title

The template's title says WAIT FOR IT. Double-click it in the Program monitor and type your own hook — three to six words that promise the payoff, such as "I fixed it in 10 seconds". Then click Safe under the monitor: keep the text inside the inner box, because YouTube's buttons and caption cover the edges and the bottom of a Short.

Want a different look? Select the title and double-click a style in Effects ▸ Text Styles, or read how to make animated text and 3D titles.

Step 4: Add captions so it works without sound

Many people scroll with the sound off. Captions keep them watching, and they make your Short accessible.

  1. Open the Captions tab and click Auto-generate. Speech recognition runs on your own device, so your audio is never uploaded.
  2. Click any caption to fix names and brand words.
  3. The template already sets large captions with a dark box, placed above YouTube's buttons. Change them with Style… if you like.

More detail: how to add subtitles to a video automatically.

Step 5: Add energy with effects and sound

A Short should change something on screen every few seconds. You don't need much:

  • Zoom Punch (beat) from Effects ▸ Creative Effects adds a quick push-in on a beat — great on a punchline.
  • A Whip Pan or Zoom In transition between two clips hides a cut and keeps the pace up.
  • Effects ▸ Sound Effects has original sounds like Whoosh, Pop and Ding. Double-click one to add it at the playhead.
  • Landscape clip that leaves empty space? Drag Background Blur Fill onto it instead of cropping.

Step 6: Make the sound clean and even

Viewers forgive a shaky shot, but not bad audio. In addition, YouTube turns loud videos down, so there is no benefit in being louder than everyone else.

  • Select your clips and choose Clip ▸ Normalize Loudness… at −14 LUFS (YouTube, Spotify and most online video).
  • Put music on its own audio track, select it and apply Effects ▸ Smart Audio ▸ Auto Duck Music Under Voice — the music dips whenever you speak.

Quiet phone audio? See how to make audio louder and clearer.

Step 7: Export your YouTube Short

  1. Click Export and choose the YouTube Shorts / Reels / TikTok (9:16) preset — 1080×1920 H.264 MP4.
  2. If you burned captions in during step 4 they are included; you can also save an .srt file.
  3. Upload the MP4 from the YouTube app or YouTube Studio. YouTube lists its current length and format rules in Upload YouTube Shorts.

Tip: Export takes seconds on most computers because Reelsmith encodes on your own graphics hardware — nothing is uploaded until you upload it yourself.

A checklist to edit YouTube Shorts that keep viewers

  • The first second shows the result or asks a question.
  • No pauses left; the picture changes every few seconds.
  • It makes sense with the sound off.
  • Text and captions sit inside the safe zone.
  • Voice is clear and the music sits underneath it.
  • It ends cleanly — a loop back to the start often gets replays.

Frequently asked questions

Can I edit YouTube Shorts on my phone?

Yes. Reelsmith works in mobile browsers with touch gestures, so you can edit and export on the same phone you filmed with. Generating captions is slower on a phone, so start with the Tiny or Base caption model.

Do I need a paid YouTube Shorts editor?

No. Everything in this guide — the template, captions, effects, loudness and the 9:16 export — is free in Reelsmith, with no watermark and no account.

Can I reuse a horizontal YouTube video as a Short?

Yes. Cut the best 15–45 seconds, then either scale the clip up to fill the 9:16 frame or apply Background Blur Fill to keep the whole picture.

Is my video uploaded while I edit?

No. Editing, captions and export run on your device. Read why your videos never leave your computer.

For more ideas, see 7 editing tips that make short videos easier to watch. Ready? Open the editor and start from the Shorts template.

posts.html:
An animated subscribe button near the start or end of a video is a simple way to grow a channel. A short "subscribe" reminder near the start or end of a video is a simple way to grow a channel. Reelsmith includes animated buttons that are ready to use, with transparent backgrounds — no green screen or background removal needed.

1. Open the Library of subscribe button animations

Click the Library tab (next to Project, Effects and Captions). You'll find:

  • Subscribe Button, Like Button, Comment Button and Notification Bell
  • Like · Comment · Subscribe (all three in one)
  • Follow Button, Share Button, Click Cursor, Bouncing Arrow and Progress Bar

Hover over a card to preview the animation.

2. Add it to the video

  • Double-click a card to add it at the playhead, or
  • drag it onto a track above your video.

It's placed on V2 or higher, sized for your frame — including vertical 9:16 videos.

3. Make it yours

Select the graphic and open Effect Controls ▸ Graphic to change the text (for example SUBSCRIBE → JOIN) and the colours. Move and resize it in the Program monitor, and drag the clip's edges on the timeline to make it stay longer or shorter.

You can also add an In, Out or Loop animation from Effects ▸ Animations — try Pop in and Pulse as a loop.

The click-and-bell sound

The Subscribe Button comes with a matching sound: a click as the cursor presses the button, then a bell as the bell icon swings. The sound is placed on an audio track and linked to the graphic, so they move together.

Don't want the sound? Select the graphic, press ⌘L (Ctrl+L on Windows) to unlink it, then click the audio clip and press Delete.

When to show it

  • After you've delivered something useful — viewers are more likely to subscribe once they've got value.
  • For 3–5 seconds, in a corner that doesn't cover faces or important text.
  • Once or twice per video, not constantly.

Tip: Have your own button animation on a white or green background? See How to remove the background from a video.

Why add a subscribe button?

Many viewers like a video but forget to subscribe. A short, friendly reminder at the right moment turns some of them into subscribers. However, timing matters: a button in the first seconds, before you have delivered anything, is easy to ignore. Instead, show it right after a useful tip or a funny moment, and then once more near the end.

Where to put the subscribe button

  • Bottom third, left or right: clear of faces and of the platform's own buttons. Click Safe in the Program monitor to see the safe zone.
  • Vertical videos: keep it above the bottom quarter, where Shorts and Reels show captions and controls.
  • The last 20 seconds of a YouTube video are usually covered by YouTube's own end screens; show your button before that.

Make it match your channel

Change the colours in Effect Controls ▸ Graphic to your brand colours and the text to your call to action — FOLLOW, JOIN or a word in your viewers' language. Pair it with a title in the same colours; see how to make animated text and 3D titles.

Using your own subscribe animation

Have a subscribe clip on a green, white or black background? Put it on V2 and right-click ▸ Remove Background. The full steps are in how to remove a video background.

Frequently asked questions

Is the subscribe button free to use?

Yes. The Library graphics and sounds are original to Reelsmith and free to use in your videos, including monetized ones.

Does it work for TikTok and Instagram?

Yes. Change the text to FOLLOW and use the Follow Button or Share Button graphics.

How long should the subscribe button stay on screen?

3–5 seconds is enough: long enough to notice, short enough not to annoy.

posts.title: How to Add Subtitles to a Video Automatically (Free, Online)
posts.metaTitle: Add Subtitles to Video Automatically, Free
posts.description: Add subtitles to video automatically: captions are made from speech on your own device, then edited, styled and burned in or saved as .srt. Free, no upload.
posts.excerpt: Generate captions from speech in your browser, edit them, and burn them into your video or export an .srt file — free and without uploading your video.
posts.imageAlt: Reelsmith Captions panel listing auto-generated subtitles above the video timeline
posts.html:
Want to add subtitles to video without typing every word? Reelsmith writes them for you from the speech in your video. The speech recognition runs on your own computer, so the audio is never uploaded — and it is free.

Captions make your videos easier to follow with the sound off, help viewers who are deaf or hard of hearing, and keep people watching longer. The W3C's guide to captions explains why they matter for accessibility.

What you need

  • A video with clear speech (or a separate voice-over track).
  • A recent version of Chrome, Edge, Safari or Firefox. Chrome and Edge are the fastest because they can use your graphics chip.

1. Put the video on the timeline

Open the editor, click New Project (or Start Editing) and drag your video onto the timeline. If the audio is on its own track, that works too — captions are made from everything you can hear.

2. Generate auto captions

  1. Open the Captions tab in the bottom-left panel and click Auto-generate. You can also use Captions ▸ Auto-generate Captions… in the menu bar.
  2. Choose what to transcribe: the Entire sequence, just the part between your In and Out points, or the selected clips.
  3. Pick the spoken language — 21 languages are listed, including English, Spanish, Hindi, Bengali and Arabic — or leave Detect automatically.
  4. Choose the accuracy. Base is a good balance; Tiny is fastest; Small is the most accurate for difficult audio and less common languages.
  5. Click Generate.

The first time, the caption engine downloads once (about 45–95 MB, depending on the model) and stays in your browser. After that it starts almost instantly.

Tip: Tick Translate the captions into English to get English subtitles from speech in another language.

3. Check and fix the automatic subtitles

Speech recognition is good but not perfect — names, brands and technical words often need a correction.

  • Click a caption in the Captions panel and edit its text.
  • Drag caption clips on the CC track to move them, or drag their edges to change how long they stay on screen.
  • Click Add at playhead to add a caption by hand.

4. Style the subtitles

Click Style… in the Captions panel to change the text size, colour, background box, position and margin so the subtitles fit your video. For short vertical videos, larger text with a dark box is easiest to read on a phone.

5. Export with subtitles

Click Export. Under Captions choose:

  • Burn into the video — the subtitles become part of the picture (best for Instagram, TikTok and Shorts).
  • Save as an .srt file only — upload it as a subtitle track on YouTube or Vimeo, where viewers can turn it on and off.
  • Burn in and save an .srt file — both.

You can also use Captions ▸ Export Captions (.srt)… at any time.

Burned-in subtitles or an .srt file?

Burned-in subtitles always show, look the same everywhere and survive re-uploads, which is why they suit short-form apps. An .srt file keeps the picture clean, lets viewers switch subtitles off, and can be indexed by video platforms. When in doubt, choose Burn in and save an .srt file and use whichever the platform needs.

Tips for accurate automatic subtitles

  • Clean the audio first. A High-Pass filter and Normalize Loudness… help the recognizer — see how to make quiet audio louder.
  • Turn the music down while generating, or generate from the voice track only by selecting it.
  • Pick the language instead of auto-detect when a video mixes languages.
  • Use Small for accents, fast speech or noisy places.

How long does it take to add subtitles to a video?

On a recent laptop with the Base model, a one-minute video usually takes well under a minute to transcribe in Chrome or Edge. In addition, the first run includes the one-time model download. As a result, longer videos are best captioned in parts: set In and Out points around each section and choose In to Out.

Correcting the text is usually the slowest part. For example, a five-minute interview might need a dozen fixes for names and brands. However, that is still much faster than typing every line yourself.

Hide captions without deleting them

Untick Show captions in the Captions panel (or click CC in the Program monitor). Hidden captions are left out of exports unless you choose Burn into the video.

Frequently asked questions

Is the automatic subtitle generator really free?

Yes. There is no account, no per-minute limit and no watermark. The speech model is open source and runs in your browser.

Is my audio uploaded to make the captions?

No. The model is downloaded once to your browser and the transcription happens on your device. You can remove it later with Captions ▸ Remove Caption Engine….

Can I add subtitles to a video on my phone?

Yes — the editor works on phones and tablets. Generating captions is slower on a phone than on a computer, so start with the Tiny or Base model.

Can I import an existing .srt file?

Yes. Choose Captions ▸ Import Captions (.srt)… or click Import .srt in the Captions panel, then edit and style them like generated ones. See Captions and subtitles.

Next, make your subtitles part of a great short video: how to make vertical videos for Shorts, Reels and TikTok.

posts.html:
A good title grabs attention in the first second. Reelsmith gives you three ways to make animated text for your videos: start from a template, apply a one-click style, or build your own look with text effects and animations. Everything runs in your browser, free.

The fastest way: a title template

Open Effects ▸ Title Templates and double-click one — for example Retro Pop 3D Title, Epic 3D Title, Kinetic Words or Bouncy Words. It's added at the playhead, sized for your frame. Double-click the text in the Program monitor to type your own words.

Other templates cover everyday needs: Lower Third for names, Chapter Title, Countdown 3-2-1, Call to Action and Breaking News Bar.

Type your own title

  1. Press T for the Type tool.
  2. Click in the Program monitor and type. Press ⌘Enter (Ctrl+Enter on Windows) or click outside to finish.
  3. Drag the text to move it; drag the corner handles to resize.
  4. Set the font, size, colour, outline, shadow and background box in Effect Controls ▸ Text.

One-click styles for animated text

With the title selected, double-click a style in Effects ▸ Text Styles: Retro Pop 3D, Epic Gold 3D, Gradient Bold, Two-Tone, Sticker Outline, Candy 3D, Gold Luxe, Comic Burst 3D, Neon, Elegant and more. Applying a new style replaces the old one, so you can try several quickly.

Build your own 3D or gradient look

Effect Controls ▸ Text Effects has:

  • Gradient fill with two colours and an angle.
  • 3D extrude with depth, direction and side colour.
  • Highlight words: wrap a word in asterisks — Make it *pop* — and it takes the highlight colour.
  • Halftone dots, outer outline, offset shadow, glow and letter spacing.

Add animated text: In, Out and Loop

Drag an animation from Effects ▸ Animations onto the title:

  • In: Pop, Zoom, Slide, Fade Up, Blur In, Bounce, Stamp, Typewriter, and text-only Words Pop, Words Rise, Letters Drop and more.
  • Out: the same moves in reverse, plus Erase.
  • Loop: Pulse, Float, Wobble, Letter Wave or Word Bounce while the title is on screen.

Each title has one In, one Out and one Loop animation. Set their duration, speed and strength in Effect Controls ▸ Animation.

Which animated text style to use

  • Hooks for Shorts and Reels: Words Pop or Bouncy Words — fast and energetic.
  • Vlogs and travel: Fade Up or Typewriter with an Elegant Serif style.
  • Tutorials and interviews: a Lower Third with a gentle Slide In.
  • Calls to action: Pop In plus a Pulse loop so it gets noticed without distracting.

Make animated text match the beat

Titles feel more professional when they appear on a beat or a sound. First, play the music and press M to add a marker on each beat. Then drag the title so it starts on a marker. Finally, add a Pop sound from Effects ▸ Sound Effects at the same point. For example, a three-word hook can pop in word by word on three beats with Words Pop.

Tips for titles that read well

  • Keep it short — three to six words.
  • Use strong contrast: a light fill with a dark outline or shadow is readable on any background. The W3C contrast guideline explains how much contrast text needs.
  • Leave a little space at the edges; click Safe in the Program monitor to see the safe zone.
  • Give viewers time to read: about one second per three words, plus the animation.

Frequently asked questions

Can I make animated text without After Effects?

posts.title: 7 Editing Tips That Make Short Videos Easier to Watch
posts.description: Seven editing tips for short videos on Shorts, Reels and TikTok: strong hooks, tight cuts, captions, on-screen text, pacing, sound and framing.
posts.excerpt: Practical, beginner-friendly editing tips for Shorts, Reels and TikTok — hooks, pacing, captions, sound and framing — with how to do each in Reelsmith.
posts.imageAlt: Applying the Zoom Punch effect to a clip, with the Effects panel searched for zoom
posts.html:
Short videos live or die in the first few seconds. These seven editing tips make a noticeable difference on YouTube Shorts, Instagram Reels and TikTok, and each one takes less than a minute in Reelsmith, the free editor that runs in your browser.

1. Start with the most interesting moment

Don't warm up. Open on the result, the punchline or the question your video answers. Drag your best clip to the start of the timeline, or trim the slow opening with the razor tool (C).

2. Cut every pause

Silences that feel natural in conversation feel slow on screen. Play through, split at the start and end of each pause with Clip ▸ Split at Playhead (⌘K), and remove the piece with Ripple Delete (⇧Delete) so the gap closes. Fast cuts like this are called jump cuts and are normal in short-form video. The waveform on audio clips shows you where the pauses are. See Deleting clips and closing gaps.

3. Add captions

Many people watch with the sound off. Generate captions automatically, correct any wrong words, and choose Burn into the video when you export.

4. Put a headline on screen

A few bold words in the first second tell viewers why they should stay. Press T, type, and apply a style from Effects ▸ Text Styles. A Words Pop animation draws the eye without being distracting. More in How to make animated text and 3D titles.

5. Change the picture every few seconds

Cut to a different angle, zoom in on the action, or add a quick transition such as Whip Pan or Zoom In. Even on a single shot, slowly keyframing Scale from 100 % to 110 % adds energy. See Effect Controls and keyframes.

6. Make the sound clean and consistent

Viewers forgive average video, but not bad audio. Use Clip ▸ Normalize Loudness… so every clip is equally loud, and Effects ▸ Smart Audio ▸ Auto Duck Music Under Voice so music never drowns out speech. Our audio tutorial covers the rest.

7. Frame for vertical screens

Keep faces and text in the middle third of a 9:16 frame, where app buttons and captions won't cover them. Click Safe in the Program monitor to see the margins. The vertical video tutorial shows how to reframe landscape footage.

Editing tips for the first three seconds

The opening decides whether people stay. For example, start mid-action rather than with a greeting, show the finished result before the steps, or put a question on screen. In addition, avoid logos and intros at the start of a short: save branding for the end. As a result, viewers see why they should keep watching straight away.

Bonus editing tips: speed, freeze and reverse

  • Speed up the boring part: select a clip and use Clip ▸ Speed/Duration… (⌘R) — 200 % for travel, 400 % for a quick time-lapse.
  • Freeze the big moment: Clip ▸ Add Frame Hold stops the picture on the playhead frame — great with a sound effect and a title.
  • Rewind for effect: Clip ▸ Reverse Clip plays a moment backwards.

Short video editing checklist before you export

  1. Does the first second show the payoff or ask a question?
  2. Are there any pauses left?
  3. Can you follow it with the sound off?
  4. Is the audio even, with music under the voice?
  5. Are faces and text inside the safe zone?

Frequently asked questions

How long should a short video be?

As short as the idea allows. Many successful Shorts and Reels are 15–30 seconds; cutting every pause usually takes a video under a minute.

What is the best free editor for short videos?

Any editor with a timeline, captions and 9:16 export will do. Reelsmith adds auto captions and vertical presets for free, with no watermark, in the browser.

Should I add music to every short?

Not always. Music helps montages; for talking videos, keep it quiet or duck it under the voice.

Put these together and even a simple phone clip feels intentional. Open the editor and try them on your next video.
